_note: Additions and corrections made in the v54 build (Nov 2026): new nodes and ties (several Rothschild, Sursock, Ottoman land-law and British-state nodes), and labels updated with today-dollar equivalents. Each new tie carries its own refs.

nodes.name: Alfred Mond, Lord Melchett
nodes.note: Alfred Mond (1868–1930), industrialist and Liberal cabinet minister under Lloyd George (First Commissioner of Works 1916–21), first chairman of Imperial Chemical Industries. Became an active Zionist: gave £10,000 (≈ $609,000 today) to Jabotinsky in 1920, toured Palestine with Weizmann in 1921, sat on the board of the Palestine Electric Corporation, and presided over the English Zionist Federation.

nodes.name: Imperial Chemical Industries (ICI)
nodes.note: Chemicals conglomerate whose first chairman was Alfred Mond.

nodes.name: Rufus Isaacs, Marquess of Reading
nodes.note: Rufus Isaacs (1860–1935): Lord Chief Justice, Viceroy of India, Foreign Secretary. Took up Zionist affairs late in life; with Mond and Herbert Samuel he was a founding chairman of the Palestine Electric Corporation and chaired it from 1926.

nodes.name: Hugo Hirst
nodes.note: Director of the General Electric Company, invited by Rutenberg to sit on the council of the Palestine Electric Corporation alongside Lord Reading and Herbert Samuel.

nodes.name: Israel Sieff
nodes.note: Israel Sieff (1889–1972), Marks & Spencer director and later chairman. Met Weizmann in 1913, served on the 1918 Zionist Commission, and with his wife Rebecca endowed the Daniel Sieff Research Institute at Rehovot (1934), later the Weizmann Institute of Science.

nodes.name: Simon Marks
nodes.note: Simon Marks (1888–1964), chairman of Marks & Spencer from 1916–17. Worked with Weizmann in negotiations with successive British governments and was a leading contributor to the Sieff Institute and the Weizmann Institute.

nodes.name: Harry Sacher
nodes.note: Manchester Guardian journalist and Zionist, brother-in-law of Marks and Sieff, later a Marks & Spencer director. His annotated draft of the Zionist text for the 1917 declaration survives.

nodes.name: Marks & Spencer
nodes.note: British retailer led by Simon Marks and Israel Sieff; the two families funded the Daniel Sieff Research Institute.

nodes.name: Daniel Sieff Research Institute (1934)
nodes.note: Research institute at Rehovot founded in 1934 at Weizmann's suggestion, endowed by Israel and Rebecca Sieff with support from the Marks and Sacher families; renamed the Weizmann Institute of Science in 1949.

nodes.name: C. P. Scott
nodes.note: C. P. Scott (1846–1932), editor and owner of the Manchester Guardian. Met Weizmann in 1914, introduced him to Lloyd George and Herbert Samuel, and backed the Jewish Legion editorially.

nodes.name: Manchester Guardian
nodes.note: Liberal daily edited by C. P. Scott; its staff included Zionist journalists Harry Sacher and Herbert Sidebotham.

nodes.name: Lloyd George, Roberts & Co. (solicitors)
nodes.note: Lloyd George's law firm, which in 1903 drafted the Uganda scheme at the request of Herzl's go-between Leopold Greenberg: Lloyd George's first working contact with the Zionist movement.

nodes.name: William Hechler
nodes.note: Anglican clergyman and chaplain at the British Embassy in Vienna; former tutor in the household of the Grand Duke of Baden. Introduced Herzl to the Grand Duke and, through him, to Kaiser Wilhelm II.

nodes.name: Frederick I, Grand Duke of Baden
nodes.note: German sovereign, uncle of Kaiser Wilhelm II. Received Herzl through Hechler and became an advocate for him with the Kaiser.

nodes.name: Adelheid de Rothschild
nodes.note: Wife of Edmond de Rothschild. Visited Jerusalem with him in 1887; the couple were reburied at Ramat HaNadiv in 1954.

nodes.name: Elie Scheid
nodes.note: Edmond's chief supervisor of the Palestine colonies 1883–1900, working from Paris; appointed inspector when colonisation began in September 1883. Assisted land purchases and marketing of the Baron's wines.

nodes.name: Yehoshua Ossowetzky
nodes.note: Senior official (1858–1929) in Edmond de Rothschild's administration in Palestine.

nodes.name: Carmel Wine Co. / Carmel Oriental
nodes.note: Export and local marketing company for the Rishon LeZion and Zikhron Ya'akov wine cellars set up by Edmond de Rothschild (Carmel name from 1896; Carmel Oriental for the Ottoman market from 1902).

nodes.name: Ottoman state sale of Marj ibn Amir (1872)
nodes.note: The Ottoman government sold the Jezreel Valley (Marj ibn Amir) to the Sursock family of Beirut in 1872 for about £20,000 (≈ $2.7 million today); the family went on to hold roughly 230,000–400,000 dunams there.

nodes.name: Elias (Ilyas) Sursock
nodes.note: Beirut Greek Orthodox banker, merchant and landowner who in 1910–11 sold about 10,000 dunams around al-Fula to the Jewish National Fund.

nodes.name: Nagib and Albert Sursock
nodes.note: Sursock family members who contracted in 1912 to sell a large Jezreel tract to the Palestine Land Development Company (stalled by the war); later sales include about 71,356 dunams with Tel Adashim.

nodes.name: Ottoman ban on land sales to Jews (1892)
nodes.note: 1892 decision to prohibit the sale of land in Palestine to Jews, including Ottoman citizens. Preceded by restrictions on Jewish immigration to Palestine from 1881–82.

nodes.name: Jerusalem notables' petition (24 June 1891)
nodes.note: Petition to the Grand Vizier demanding an end to Russian-Jewish immigration and a ban on land acquisition; described as the first organised Arab protest against Zionist settlement.

nodes.name: Muhammad Tahir al-Husayni
nodes.note: Mufti of Jerusalem (1842–1908), chaired the Commission for Sale; used delay and bureaucratic obstruction against land sales to Jews, per a scholarly survey citing a German consul's complaint of May 1893.

nodes.name: FO 78/4476: British Jews' petition on the Ottoman ban (1893)
nodes.note: Foreign Office correspondence forwarding petitions from British-subject Jews in Jerusalem complaining of Ottoman regulations barring them from buying and selling real estate, and asking for protection.

nodes.name: Zadok Kahn
nodes.note: Chief Rabbi of France. Received Yusuf Diya al-Khalidi's 1 March 1899 letter and showed it to Herzl. Whether he advised Edmond de Rothschild is not established in the sources pulled this pass.

nodes.name: Khalidi letter to Zadok Kahn (1 Mar 1899)
nodes.note: Seven-page letter in French from the mayor of Jerusalem warning that Zionism would collide with the existing population, written for passing on to Herzl. Often quoted for one line granting the Jews' historical tie, but it ends by urging that Palestine be left alone. Herzl replied 19 March 1899.

nodes.name: Ottoman Public Debt Administration (1881)
nodes.note: Created by the Decree of Muharrem (Dec 1881) to collect revenues for European bondholders; run by creditor representatives (British/Dutch/Belgian, French, German, Austrian, Italian, Ottoman holders and the Ottoman Bank). Employed thousands of officials, at times more than the finance ministry.

nodes.name: Société de la Régie des Tabacs (1883)
nodes.note: Tobacco monopoly to which the OPDA farmed out Ottoman tobacco revenue on 27 May 1883. The syndicate included the Ottoman Bank, the Rothschild family's Vienna Creditanstalt and Bleichröder of Berlin.

nodes.name: Creditanstalt (Vienna)
nodes.note: Vienna bank described in the source as the Rothschild family's; a member of the 1883 tobacco Régie syndicate.

nodes.name: Herzl–Abdülhamid audience (15 May 1901)
nodes.note: Herzl proposed consolidating the Ottoman public debt in exchange for a charter for Jewish settlement in Palestine. The Sultan gave him decorations, not a charter.

nodes.name: Najib Nassar
nodes.note: Haifa Christian journalist (1865–1947/48). Founded al-Karmil in 1908; published the first Arabic book on Zionism (1911); in 1914 urged pressure on Arab landowners not to sell.

nodes.name: Al-Karmil (newspaper, Haifa, 1908)
nodes.note: Weekly founded by Najib Nassar. Its early line favoured the Ottoman authorities; by 1911 it opposed the Committee of Union and Progress over perceived bias toward Zionism.

nodes.name: Al-Fula affair (1910–11)
nodes.note: Sale of lands around al-Fula to the Jewish National Fund, alongside a rumour that Lebanese landlord Najib al-Asfar's bid for a 95-year crown-lands lease was a Zionist front. Triggered a wave of Arab press opposition.

nodes.name: Najib Ibrahim al-Asfar
nodes.note: Lebanese landowner who sought a 95-year lease of crown lands in Palestine and Syria in 1910; a false rumour said he was acting for Zionists.

nodes.name: Sursuq Family Archive (USEK, Lebanon)
nodes.note: Family archive at the Phoenix Center, Holy Spirit University of Kaslik, with papers of buyers and sellers. A primary source to pull for the land sales.

nodes.name: Eviction of Jezreel tenants
nodes.note: Sursock sales are credited with the eviction of 8,730 tenants, a figure attributed to the Shaw Commission.

nodes.name: Land Transfer Ordinance (1920)
nodes.note: First Mandate-era land transfer law, 1 Oct 1920. Sources disagree on its effect: one says it removed Ottoman-era restrictions on sales to Jews, others stress consent and tenant-protection rules.

nodes.name: Land Transfers Regulations (1940)
nodes.note: Divided Palestine into zones restricting transfers from Arabs to non-Arabs (heaviest in Zone A), issued under the 1939 Order-in-Council. Municipal areas were exempt.

nodes.name: Land Transfer Inquiry Committee (1945)
nodes.note: British inquiry into transfers under the 1940 regulations. The Jewish Agency declined to take part.

nodes.name: JNF Blue Box (small-donor tins)
nodes.note: Collection tins used by the Jewish National Fund from its start. A US archive finding aid says more than half of the land the JNF owned by 1948 was bought with Blue Box proceeds (single source, not independently checked).

nodes.name: JNF land holdings by year
nodes.note: JNF land: 22,363 dunams by 1920, 516,000 by 1940, 936,000 by May 1948 (PIJ). The 936,000 dunams were about 54% of land held by Jews and under 4% of Mandate Palestine; a further 800,000 dunams were held by other Jewish bodies and individuals.

nodes.name: PICA land holdings (about 500,000 dunams, 1934)
nodes.note: A 1934 JTA report, already cited on this map's PICA tie, puts PICA at about 500,000 dunams, about twice the JNF's holdings then. PICA's land went to the JNF in 1957-58. Against roughly 1.74 million dunams held by Jews in 1948 (936,000 JNF plus 800,000 others) that is on the order of 29%; this mixes 1934 and 1948 figures and is a rough estimate.

nodes.name: Keren Hayesod funds raised, 1920-1948
nodes.note: Encyclopaedia Judaica table: $143,000,000 raised 1920-1948 (nominal; ≈ $3.6 billion today, midpoint-year estimate). A second account, citing Eliezer Kaplan (1946), says over £14.5 million by 1945 (≈ $1.2 billion today, midpoint-year estimate). The two do not reconcile and are left side by side.

nodes.name: Jewish capital formation in Mandate Palestine
nodes.note: Jewish capital was about 60% of Palestine's fixed capital formation by the end of the Mandate, with Jews investing 39.3% of their GNP a year between the wars, largely private capital brought by immigrants (Metzer via Stein). Capital in Jewish industries rose from £4.39 million (≈ $469 million today) in 1939 to £12.09 million (≈ $994 million today) by 1942.

nodes.name: Diaspora money in 1948
nodes.note: One secondary account puts diaspora contributions in 1948 at $250 million (≈ $3.5 billion today), with about 75% of the war's cost raised inside Israel. Single source, not independently checked.

jct.note: Decided at the Second Zionist Congress (1898); incorporated under English Companies Acts, March 20, 1899. Authorized capital £2,000,000 in £1 shares. Actual result: roughly 250,000 shares sold worldwide (~£250,000 (≈ $49 million today) raised) — far below target. Its stated aim was to acquire the capital and a "charter" to enable large-scale settlement in Palestine.

apc_bank.note: Founded as a JCT subsidiary, February 27, 1902, initial capital ~£50,000 (≈ $9.4 million today). Chairman: David Wolffsohn; manager: Zalman David Levontin (a founder of Rishon LeZion, 1882). First branch opened in Jaffa, 1903; expanded to Jerusalem, Beirut, Hebron, Haifa, Safed, Tiberias, Gaza by 1914. Renamed Anglo-Palestine Bank c.1930; became Bank Leumi in 1950–51.

keren_hayesod.note: Founded at the London Zionist conference, December 24, 1920, as the WZO's central, permanent fundraising arm — open to non-Zionist donors as well. Originators: Hillel Zlatopolsky and Isaac Naiditch. Registered in Britain 1921; headquarters moved to Jerusalem 1926. Original five-year target: £25,000,000 (≈ $2.3 billion today).

james_armand.note: After 1948 the documented Rothschild money in Israel ran through visible institutions: PICA's land passed to the JNF (1957-58); Yad Hanadiv; the Knesset building (£1.25M (≈ $36 million today) bequest, 1966). No document found shows Rothschild ownership or control of the Bank of Israel, which is state-owned and created by Knesset law in 1954.

us_congress.note: Congress passed resolutions of support (1922 Lodge-Fish, the 1945 concurrent resolution) but never voted to create or recognize a state; those were executive acts. Named champions: Lodge, Fish, Wagner, Taft, Wright, Compton, Celler, Bloom; two-thirds of the Senate joined the American Palestine Committee. No documented campaign money from Zionist organizations to members of Congress before 1948 was found in the sources checked; the documented levers were letters, telegrams, platform planks and votes. The one documented campaign money in this map is Feinberg and Kaufmann's $100,000 (≈ $1.4 million today) for Truman in 1948.

exim.note: Among the dollar flows the record documents between 1921 and 1949, the Feinberg–Kaufmann money is the smallest, about a tenth of a million dollars beside a $100 million (≈ $1.4 billion today) Export-Import Bank loan of 1949 and tens of millions raised for arms.

stalin.note: Deliveries included some 35,000 German-pattern Karabiner 98k rifles and heavy weapons, many produced for the Wehrmacht; a 1952 report by Czechoslovak Foreign Minister Viliam Široký put receipts at almost $14.5 million (≈ $201 million today). Czechoslovakia, communist since the February 1948 coup, sold with Soviet consent while Britain supplied the Arab air forces and the US kept its embargo.
